study.title: Numbers 27 - Heritage, succession and direction of the people
study.overview: The chapter brings together three scenes linked to the continuity of Israel in the desert and the promised land. First, the daughters of Zelofeade ask that the father's inheritance not disappear because he has no male children, and God confirms that the case of them reveals a principle of justice for the transmission of property within the family. Then the Lord tells Moses that he will see the land, but he will not enter it, because in Meribah he has failed to sanctify it before the people. Finally, Moses asks that Israel not be without leadership and God indicates Joshua, with the laying on of hands and public ordination before Eleazar and the congregation.

outline.title: The daughters of Zelofed and the rule of inheritance
outline.explanation: The five sisters present themselves before Israel's leadership and argue that his father's name should not disappear just because he died without male children. Moses brings the question to the Lord, who approves their request and turns that case into a standard for Israel: in the absence of sons, the inheritance passes to the daughter; in the lack of daughter, to the brothers; then to the brothers of the father; and, finally, to the closest relative of the family.

outline.title: Moses is warned of his next death
outline.explanation: God sends Moses to go up to Mount Abarim to look upon the promised land, but he also tells him that he will be gathered to his people as Aaron. The reason is sin in Meribah, where Moses and Aaron did not sanctify the Lord before the congregation. The text preserves both the mercy of allowing the vision of the earth and the seriousness of the leader's disobedience.

outline.title: The choice and the investiture of Joshua
outline.explanation: Moses responds with prayer for the continuity of the people: he asks the Lord to raise up a man to lead the congregation as a shepherd leads the flock. God chooses Joshua, describes him as someone in whom there is spirit, and commands Moses to present him publicly, to lay his hands on him and to give him part of his dignity. Moses obeys, establishing a succession visible and recognized by the whole community.

study.context: The chapter shows Israel's organized life as the people of the covenant, with decisions given at the door of the tabernacle and before the priestly and civil authorities. It is not just about private issues: inheritance, leadership, and obedience to the Lord affect the whole community. The text also anticipates the transition from one generation to another, when the people are at the doors of the promised land and need an internal order to move forward.
study.theology: The chapter teaches that God governs not only the great events, but also the daily justice of the community. The inheritance cannot be treated as a simple extension of male power; the Lord hears the cry of the daughters of Zelophehad and affirms a principle of equity within the covenant. At the same time, the leader's sin is not relativized: Moses remains a faithful servant, but his failure in Meribah brings real consequences. Finally, leadership in Israel is not born of personal ambition; it is granted by God, publicly confirmed and linked to the Spirit and priestly mediation. Joshua's succession also shows that God's work continues beyond the death of a great leader. In evangelical reading, the chapter highlights God's faithfulness in preserving his people, instructing him in justice and providing conduct when the previous generation passes.

scholarViews.insight: The daughters presented their case to the largest authorities of Israel at the entrance of the tabernacle, seeking an exception to the current law and bringing the issue to the most important public place for meaningful decisions.
Moses, although he could not receive relief for himself, zealously asked that the work of God continue and that the people would not be without direction as sheep without a shepherd.
The laying on of hands on Joshua worked as a sign that he had been assigned and qualified for the task, publicly receiving the task of leading the people.

questions: What does God's answer to the daughters of Zelophehad reveal about their concern for righteousness within his people?
How does the discipline applied to Moses teach that spiritual leadership does not exempt anyone from accounting to God?
How does Moses' prayer for a successor challenge us to think more about our name than in the continuity of God's work?
study.practice: This chapter calls the church to unite justice, humility and continuity. In concrete terms, it is worth reviewing how we treat people in apparently secondary situations, taking their causes seriously and without favoritism. He also reminds us of confessing sins soberly, without minimizing the consequences of disobedience. And it teaches us to form successors with prayer, public recognition and responsible transmission of tasks, so that God's work depends not only on one generation or an isolated leader.
study.uncertainty: The biblical text does not explain in detail all the legal procedures of the inheritance nor does it develop the rite of the laying on of hands beyond what is narrated here. The notes provided suggest interpretive readings about the public function of the tabernacle's entrance, on the separation between military and spiritual leadership and Joshua's symbolism, but these points should be read as explanations of commentators, not as statements explicitly developed by the chapter.
